posts.text: The mascot was born around November 2016 when I asked my #Dota2 friend @dopatwo for an illustration to put on Mastodon's error page. It was meant to be a homage to Twitter's "fail whale". As you can see, the design of the mascot has changed considerably in ten years. It was cute then, but more realistic, less round. I much prefer the contemporary design, and the fact that it's not a single character.

media.alt: A beige, somewhat realistically shaped Mastodon being carried in a net by a flock of red birds.

posts.author: Eugen Rochko
posts.text: It's interesting that my bio as seen in the demo said "Developer of Mastodon, a GNU social alternative". That was the level of my ambition at the time: GNU social had a niche, tiny as it may in the grand scheme of things, and it appealed to me, so I just wanted to make something that would be nicer to use. (My original intent was making a TweetDeck-like app for GNU social, but I quickly pivoted into writing my own backend because GNU social's API was a mess and I like things to be neat).

posts.author: Eugen Rochko
posts.text:
There is a little time capsule of the UI as it was on that exact day, as I recorded a demo video for the Product Hunt submission. You can see how some UI concepts have persisted to this day, even as the details and level of refinement changed. You can also see the original blue accent color... I took that color palette from a website where people posted various color palettes, I do not remember its name anymore.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YO1jQ8_rAMU

posts.author: Eugen Rochko
posts.text: The codebase has been about 6 months in the works at that point (the first git commit was dated March 16, 2016) and mastodon.social had been running for a while too, since it was my way of testing how the federation works with other fediverse servers (and software, like GNU social) at the time. The API was the very first thing I worked on, and some of those API methods are still literally unchanged today, but the UI had already gone through multiple iterations by October 5.

posts.author: Eugen Rochko
posts.text: At that point I was 23, freshly graduated from university with a B.Sc. in Informatics, living with my parents, and freelancing on the side (I had a freelancing career in web design since high school and went to university just to get a degree). I was able to save a lot from my student loan as well, so I had the opportunity to experiment with this open-source side project.

posts.author: Eugen Rochko
posts.text: Heh. I misremembered the date--thought it was today, but looks like it was October 5. On that day, 10 years ago, I posted a link to Mastodon on Hacker News, with the title "Show HN: A new decentralized microblogging platform". That it made it to the front page ended up bringing the first 5,000 users, setting the project on the trajectory it's on today.

The NFL is urging the Supreme Court to hear New Jersey’s case over whether states can regulate prediction markets, complaining that Kalshi refused to ban easily manipulated bets and expressing concerns over consumer protection and game integrity.

#crypo #cryptocurrency #USpol #USpolitics #CitationNeededNewsletter

media.alt:
In prediction markets
As New Jersey petitions the Supreme Court to take up the issue of whether state gambling laws should apply to prediction markets, it’s found a new ally in the National Football League. The NFL filed an amicus brief urging the Court to take up the case, arguing that sports contracts in prediction markets create new risk, rather than hedge existing risk, and therefore should be regulated by state gambling commissions. They detail complaints around Kalshi’s refusal to comply with their requests to ban bets that are easily manipulated, those involving injuries or referees, and those whose outcomes can be known in advance. They also note that Kalshi’s platform allows participants who are 18 or older, despite many state gambling laws that restrict betting to 21 and older.16

Unlike Major League Baseball and the National Hockey League, which have signed sponsorship or trademark deals with prediction markets, the NFL has been more hesitant. NFL games have drawn huge volumes on prediction markets, with the league’s games accounting for $1.8 billion of the $3.3 billion total prediction market volume on the first Sunday of the most recent NFL season. According to their brief, this is all the more reason for the NFL to worry about the emergence of such platforms, which they say undermine efforts to protect bettors, ensure wagers are fair, and limit threats to the integrity of the games themselves.16

Daniel Wallach, a gaming lawyer who focuses on sports betting, said that the NFL’s encouragement “meaningfully” increases the chances the Supreme Court will hear the case. He added, “It is extremely telling that the sports league which has most forcefully advocated for federal regulation is essentially saying ‘this ain’t it’.”17

Hex founder Richard Heart, who the SEC once accused of spending investor money on sports cars, luxury watches, and the world’s largest black diamond, has been arrested in Istanbul after nearly two years on an Interpol Red Notice over Finnish tax fraud charges. He no longer faces SEC enforcement after the agency effectively dropped his case last year.

#crypo #cryptocurrency #USpol #USpolitics #CitationNeededNewsletter

media.alt:
Richard Heart
Richard Heart, the founder of the Hex cryptocurrency scheme, managed to spend nearly two years subject to an Interpol Red Notice before authorities finally nabbed him in Türkiye. The US SEC sued Heart in 2023, noting that asking people to “sacrifice” rather than “invest” their crypto assets in exchange for his PulseChain and Hex tokens was not the get-out-of-securities-laws-free card he seemed to think it was. The lawsuit further alleged he had misappropriated at least $12 million to buy sports cars, luxury watches, and the largest black diamond in the world [I35, 45, 73].11

Photograph of a woman in side profile holding The Enigma black diamond in front of her face. It is an asymmetrical faceted diamond about the size of an egg.
Caption: Heart purchased “The Enigma” for £3.16 million (then around $4.28 million) in February 2022 (via Sotheby’s)

Then, in September 2024, he was accused by Finnish authorities of evading several hundred million euros in taxes, and was named as a suspect in a brutal physical assault on a sixteen-year-old perpetrated in February 2021 [I67].12 At Finland’s request, Heart was added to the EU’s Most Wanted list and an Interpol Red Notice was issued [I72].

Turkish police have now arrested Heart and his wife in Istanbul. While a report from Turkish media outlet the Daily Sabah claims that Heart was wanted by Interpol on crypto fraud charges, the red notice only lists a charge of aggravated tax fraud.1314

Photograph: Richard Heart, wearing a top hat and speaking into a microphone
Caption: Richard Heart

Though Heart is certainly facing serious criminal consequences internationally, his US regulatory woes have eased. In February 2025, a federal judge dismissed the SEC’s lawsuit against Heart, finding the agency hadn’t adequately established that Heart had sufficient ties to the US. Heart thanked Trump for the outcome. Neither Trump nor his gutted SEC had anything to do with that ruling, but Heart may have had something to thank them for later on: in April 2025, the agency declined to amend its complaint to address the jurisdictional issues, effectively abandoning the case as it had so many others against crypto firms [I78, 82].

While these events are intended to juice the token’s price — which has already plummeted more than 95% from its highs — they have become increasingly ineffective, producing shorter and less dramatic price spikes.

Crypto super PAC Fairshake announced 32 House endorsements: all incumbents, all but four in safe seats. It’s their attempt to pad their win rate and claim it proves the existence of a crypto voter bloc, but they are abandoning reliable allies in tough races.

#crypo #cryptocurrency #USpol #USpolitics #CitationNeededNewsletter

media.alt: Map of the United States showing photos of the 32 House members endorsed by the crypto super PAC Fairshake, each placed on their home state. Red borders mark the 19 Republicans: Ben Cline (Virginia), Troy Downing (Montana), Tom Emmer (Minnesota), Michelle Fischbach (Minnesota), Scott Fitzgerald (Wisconsin), Mike Haridopolos (Florida), Pat Harrigan (North Carolina), French Hill (Arkansas), Bill Huizenga (Michigan), Brian Jack (Georgia), Frank Lucas (Oklahoma), Lisa McClain (Michigan), August Pfluger (Texas), Guy Reschenthaler (Pennsylvania), David Rouzer (North Carolina), Austin Scott (Georgia), Jason Smith (Missouri), Bryan Steil (Wisconsin), and Glenn Thompson (Pennsylvania). Blue borders mark the 13 Democrats: Pete Aguilar (California), Brendan Boyle (Pennsylvania), Janelle Bynum (Oregon), Josh Gottheimer (New Jersey), Steven Horsford (Nevada), Jonathan Jackson (Illinois), Lucy McBath (Georgia), Sarah McBride (Delaware), Jimmy Panetta (California), Hillary Scholten (Michigan), Terri Sewell (Alabama), Suhas Subramanyam (Virginia), and Derek Tran (California).

In elections and political influence
The crypto industry’s flagship super PAC, Fairshake, has announced a list of 32 House candidates it plans to back in the midterms. All of them are incumbents; 13 are Democrats, and 19 are Republicans. All but four are in races dubbed “safe” for them by the Cook Political Report.5

PAC spokesperson Geoff Vetter gave the game away when he bragged to The Hill, “We’ve won 53 of the 57 races we engaged in this cycle”.6 As I’ve noted previously [I68, 70, 108], the crypto PACs and advocacy groups often support shoo-in candidates so that they can later claim that their win rate reflects some silent majority of Americans who support the “crypto agenda”. Similarly, when Coinbase-linked Stand With Crypto endorsed 39 candidates in 2024, The Hill estimated prior to Election Day that 32 of them had a 75% or higher chance of winning [I68].

Out of their list, the Fairshake network has so far spent the most on Republicans Bill Huizenga (MI, $1.5 million) and French Hill (AR, $1.4 million). It has spent around $1 million apiece supporting Bryan Steil (R-WI), Janelle Bynum (D-OR), Derek Tran (D-CA), and Steven Horsford (D-NV), and $512,000 each on Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) and Pete Aguilar (D-CA). Most of the other endorsed candidates have so far received around $75,000 each from the network. Some of the biggest checks went to members who chair the committees with jurisdiction over crypto, including Hill (Financial Services) and Steil (digital assets subcommittee).

Conspicuously missing are several reliable crypto allies in tougher races, including Democrats Don Davis (NC) and Shomari Figures (AL) and Republicans Zach Nunn (IA) and Mike Lawler (NY). Fairshake spent more than $2 million each on Davis and Figures in 2024, and $1 million on Nunn; it didn’t back Lawler. Nunn and Lawler have, however, received smaller amounts of support this cycle from Andreessen Horowitz, one of Fairshake’s biggest backers, through donations by several executives to a crypto-themed joint fundraising committee called “Hodl the Line”.

Community bankers are suing the OCC over its spree of national trust bank charters, at least 13 of 21 of which went to crypto firms (including Trump’s World Liberty). They argue it’s a side door for crypto firms to get the perks of a bank charter without the rules.

#crypo #cryptocurrency #USpol #USpolitics #CitationNeededNewsletter

media.alt:
In regulators
The Independent Community Bankers of America has sued the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency over its recent rulemaking and its spree of national trust bank charters. At least 13 of the 21 charters granted by the OCC under Trump have gone to crypto firms, including Circle, Ripple, and the Trump family’s own World Liberty Financial [I88, 98, 99, 101, 102, 107]. While the national trust bank framework is intended to let firms hold assets on clients’ behalf without the more stringent oversight applied to traditional banks that take deposits and lend them out, the community banks argue that the OCC has overstepped its authority and turned the regime into a backdoor for crypto companies to get the perks of a bank charter without the rules. The suit singles out Protego, which won conditional approval for a trust charter despite plans to offer crypto custody, trading, lending, and asset management services.

The OCC’s expansion “creates a gaping hole in regulation,” the trade group writes, letting crypto firms perform many of the same functions as community banks “while evading the fundamental safeguards, obligations, and oversight of those banks.” Their customers don’t receive the protections of deposit insurance, the separation of banking and commerce, or limits on dealings with risky investments like hedge funds. And because the national charters preempt state law, they lose some state consumer protections. Many won’t realize it: “Customers will reasonably assume that a company having ‘national bank’ in its title is an insured depository institution.”

There’s also very little precedent for what will happen if one of these firms fails. “The OCC has not managed an uninsured bank receivership in nearly one hundred years,” the lawsuit points out, warning that “failures of risky uninsured national trust banks could spread instability throughout the nation’s financial system, including by spreading contagion risks to other traditional banks like community banks.”

The suit also echoes some of the same arguments raised by community banks during the Clarity Act negotiations: that crypto firms, freed from much of the regulatory burden banks carry, will siphon deposits away from community banks and reduce their capacity to lend [I91, 99, 107, 108, 110].

ICBA President and CEO Rebeca Romero Rainey said in a statement that “Congress did not create the national trust charter as a side door into the banking system for crypto firms seeking the credibility of a federal bank charter.” But crypto firms have previously balked at complaints from traditional banks. Last spring, Coinbase’s then-Chief Legal Officer Paul Grewal accused the ICBA of protectionism, writing, “Imagine opposing a regulated trust charter because you prefer crypto to stay … unregulated” [I96, 102].a

A Senate subcommittee is probing Tether’s ties to Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick supposedly divested from by handing it to his sons. Per Senator Blumenthal, Cantor’s 5% stake in Tether has skyrocketed from $600M to ~$10B since Trump returned to office.

#crypo #cryptocurrency #USpol #USpolitics #CitationNeededNewsletter

media.alt:
Tether, Howard Lutnick, and Cantor Fitzgerald
Hines isn’t the only Trump official whose ties to Tether are drawing scrutiny. The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations is probing the relationship between the stablecoin firm and financial giant Cantor Fitzgerald, which was previously headed by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Upon his cabinet appointment, Lutnick claimed to have satisfied his ethics requirements by transferring his interest in the firm to a trust benefiting his four children, and handing control to two of his sons — a move borrowed from Trump. Like Trump, Lutnick has continued to profit from the family business — his 2025 financial disclosure reported a $192 million distribution from the firm. Nor does he seem to have stepped away from it: in April, when the Cantor-funded Fellowship PAC disclosed plans to spend $1.75 million backing Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate primary runoff, senior Republican officials called Lutnick to complain. The PAC quietly dropped the ad three days later [I105].

An October 8 letter from PSI Ranking Member Richard Blumenthal to Cantor Chairman and CEO Brandon Lutnick disclosed that the subcommittee is investigating Cantor Fitzgerald’s relationship with Tether and its connections to the Trump regime.4 Cantor took a 5% stake in the stablecoin issuer in 2024, and according to Blumenthal, “Since the President’s return to office, Cantor Fitzgerald’s five percent stake in Tether has increased in value from $600 million to an estimated $10 billion, in addition to the tens of millions of dollars the company collects every year from the assets it holds for Tether.” The letter raises concerns about Tether’s use by illicit actors, including Iran’s shadow banking system, and about Cantor’s close ties to Lutnick and the rest of the Trump administration.

Blumenthal requested information on Cantor Fitzgerald’s due diligence on Tether’s reserves and anti-money laundering programs, the terms of a loan from Tether to Howard Lutnick that may have financed his transfer of the business to his children [I103], and copies of any communications by Secretary Lutnick involving regulatory matters or with other White House advisors.4

While Bo Hines shaped the Genius Act as Trump’s crypto council director, his family’s consulting firm took $6.3M+ from Tether. He pushed a change to the law that would primarily benefit Tether, then left to run Tether’s US arm.

#crypo #cryptocurrency #USpol #USpolitics #CitationNeededNewsletter

media.alt:
In the White House
Tether, Bo Hines, and NXUM
Bo Hines, President Trump’s bizarre choice [I72] to serve as the first executive director of his crypto advisory council, was among the key architects of the Genius Act, the stablecoin law signed in July 2025. Hines’ previous qualifications consisted of playing college football, losing two Congressional races, and co-owning a small consulting firm called NXUM with his father. He kept his stake in NXUM when he joined the administration.

The Wall Street Journal has now reported that weeks after Hines began working on the bill, his father and their fellow NXUM co-owner Gary Dennis met with Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino. Tether is the largest stablecoin issuer, and had the most riding on the legislation. Though NXUM previously had little involvement with the crypto sector, it pitched Tether on a “strategic lobbying” and PR campaign that has netted NXUM at least $6.3 million to date, with payments that began while Hines was still at the White House and were split three ways among the co-owners. The final deal omitted any mention of lobbying, and was routed through a separate marketing firm.

Meanwhile, Hines pushed legislators to double the grace period for crypto exchanges to stop offering noncompliant stablecoins — a change that primarily benefited Tether. He also remained active in Signal chats with his NXUM partners. When some Republican congresspeople stalled the bill, his father informed Dennis he’d gotten a “very worried” call from Ardoino and that Tether wanted them to “obliterate” the holdouts. Hours later, Hines sent the NXUM group chat talking points casting the legislators as “undermining the president and ... bought and paid for by democratic shills like coinbase and a16z”. When Trump brokered a deal with the holdouts weeks later, Dennis bragged to an associate, “Bo got it done.” Three weeks after the bill was signed, Hines left the White House; the following month, he was named CEO of Tether’s new US arm.

NXUM has only grown more entangled with Tether since. The consulting firm, which is pitching investors on a deal in which Tether would buy a 25% stake for $56 million, has started branding itself as the “strategic media infrastructure layer behind Tether”. It also helped launch the Fellowship PAC, which is chaired by Jesse Spiro, Tether US’s head of government affairs [Tether PAC]. The PAC is funded almost entirely by Cantor Fitzgerald, an investor in Tether and its primary US financial partner, which was previously run by now-Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The PAC has paid NXUM more than $6.5 million. Before it launched, Dennis reminded an associate: “Again, no link to Tether, Nxum, Bo”.

Hines was succeeded on the crypto council by Patrick Witt, whose resume likewise featured college football and failed congressional bids [I90]. Witt took over negotiations on the Clarity Act crypto market structure bill, which recently fizzled after falling short of the votes needed for cloture [I110]. In July, the council’s deputy director, Harry Jung, stepped down to join (you guessed it!) NXUM.1 Now, Witt has left his post, presumably to collect his reward. I look forward to learning who’s paying it.

His departure adds to growing nerves in the crypto sector that the White House is losing interest. David Sacks stepped down from his combined “AI and crypto czar” role in March, and earlier this month Trump tapped Jay Clayton to become his AI czar.2 No crypto czar has been named, and the digital assets advisory council is now without a director or deputy director. The Clarity Act is dead, with little hope of being revived after the midterms. If I were among the crypto executives whose money has fueled more than $250 million in super PAC election spending since 2024, I might also be a little worried that the administration got what it needed from me and is now moving on to newer, shinier things.3

Here's 3 surprising new preprints on the Atlantic ocean circulation #AMOC. 🌊The first by Winkelbauer et al. analyses 17 different ocean reanalysis products and finds the AMOC has weakened about 15% over the last 3 decades.
https://egusphere.copernicus.org/preprints/2026/egusphere-2026-5435/

The 2nd by Bell et al. from UK Met Office does a similar analysis using atmospheric reanalysis, deriving #AMOC changes from an energy balance and the heat flux though the ocean surface. The find about 14% AMOC weakening over the past 3 decades.
https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-10854125/v1

A study by Ben-Yami et al. looks for tell-tale signs of approaching an #AMOC tipping point in historic runs of climate models vs. observed SST patterns. They find a loss of stability in the real-world AMOC but not in models, so AMOC in models may be too stable.
https://journals.plos.org/climate/article?id=10.1371/journal.pclm.0000781

Now, excited public conversation (and in particular, public conversation on X) is no
substitute for actual regulation. Congress has a long history of introducing tech regulations
that go nowhere — and of launching probes that go nowhere. And if Christiano's best
efforts at getting OpenAl to self-regulate fall short — well, he won't be the first board
member to have that experience.
Still, I can't help but be heartened by the vibe shift in Al safety. Last month, in the wake of
Mark Zuckerberg's glad-handing treatise on "personal superintelligence," | argued that true
superintelligence is a dragon. And while I remain hopeful that it can be tamed, I believe the
researchers who say we are nowhere close to being sure of it — and are quitting, in protest,
jobs that would make them rich. The right people are now listening to them, and here's
hoping they take action.

posts.text: I wrote about why the AI labs make for lousy messengers about AI safety — and about why we should take them seriously anyway https://www.platformer.news/openai-astra-warning-alignment-monitoring-pachocki/

were. Is this truly the world's problem to solve, or is it primarily OpenAl's?
There's the persistent belief that, whatever safety lapses a case like the Hugging Face
incident might reveal, the attention nonetheless benefits OpenAl and the Al industry at
large. OpenAl in particular has played into this by arguing that you should respond to the
Hugging Face attack by using more OpenAl products — a case that Greg Brockman made
explicitly, in a blog post. When labs dismiss the idea that they are turning these incidents
into marketing campaigns — well, they're not not using them in marketing campaigns.

posts.author: Casey Newton
posts.text: Wrote about Meta's ludicrous effort to position itself as a leader in child safety after today's $17 billion settlement with state AGs https://www.platformer.news/meta-child-safety-settlement-instagram-facebook-youtube-tiktok/

media.alt:
This — along with countless other documented harms — is the actual history of Meta's
treatment of its child users: as a precious resource to be mined, monetized, and analyzed
well beyond what the law allows. No wonder, then, that as of last month, nearly six in 10
Americans support banning under-16s from social media entirely. At least 10 countries have
passed or implemented such bans already, and more are likely to follow.
Viewed in that light, Meta's belated announcement of new limits and safety features is
hardly the "groundbreaking" agreement Mahoney describes it as. Rather, it's a bet that
accepting a small amount of pain will let the company avoid a much larger one. Given the
thousands of lawsuits the company still faces around the country, though, Meta still may be
in for a world of hurt.

posts.text: I wrote about building an LLM wiki to stay on top of my beat. A month in, it's changing how I work https://www.platformer.news/karpathy-llm-wiki-journalism-productivity/

media.alt:
The result is that I now have more than 1,440 wiki pages covering most of what has ever
interested me at Platformer: from the content moderation focus of the first few years to my
growing interest in child safety and Al progress. The wiki creates detailed timelines that link
to original sources, and I can ask it questions using a simple Obsidian plugin named
Claudian.
How does this make me more productive? I've found it highly useful in fast-evolving,
complex cases like the OpenAl / Hugging Face agentic breach, where we learned a little
more about the story every few days for a matter of weeks. Each day as I prepared to
write, or podcast, or go on someone else's podcast, I would pull up the page and refresh my
memory — while also opening up the original sources to make sure nothing I was about to
say was hallucinated. Given the real complexity of that story - how exactly did the agent
escape? From where? To where? — this saved me tons of time.

posts.text: Town was the first company I saw in a while that made me say ohhhh ... everyone is going to copy this. I interviewed 'mayor' Jean-Denis Greze about building a self-organizing company https://www.platformer.news/town-interview-jean-denis-greze-assistants/

media.alt:
Newton: Every once in a while, when I'm using productivity software, I have one of these
moments where I think: oh, everyone is going to copy this. And I had that when I saw this
wiki that you built for your customers. Tell us a little about it.
Greze: We cannot claim that the wiki is our original idea — Karpathy and others have talked
about how you can use Al to take a set of documents and build a knowledge base out of
them. Our job is to take this incredible technology and make it accessible to everyone. We
had the wiki in the background for a long time as something that powers the experience —
and it turns out people love reading about themselves, so at some point it just became
natural to expose it.
The single-person version of this is interesting. The multi-person version is even more
interesting. You're talking about building this new company — it's not just what it knows
about each person, which is private information for each person. The company has things
about the business as a whole that everyone could use knowing. Can you do that
automatically? Most companies aren't even on Notion — I love Notion, it's a fantastic
product, but in the world of productivity, it's like 1 percent of companies that are on
something like Notion. How could you give that kind of power to 99 percent of companies,
where it can have a really good understanding of what's happening across the business, so
that everyone can be more effective in their role?

posts.author: Casey Newton
posts.text: I wrote about Mark Zuckerberg's facile, self-serving AI manifesto and what he misunderstands about the technology https://www.platformer.news/zuckerberg-ai-manifesto-dragons/

media.alt:
Zuckerberg pays glancing attention to risks, suggesting that we adjust mitigation strategies
if Al enables new biological attacks, and proposes monitoring if labs achieve recursive self-
improvement and loss-of-control risks grow exponentially.
But nowhere does he explain how his framework would handle a harm we can't iterate our
way out of: an engineered pandemic, say, or a catastrophic cyberattack. He casts falling
behind China as the risk that dwarfs all others, and suggests that any precaution that slows
down US releases by even a month itself is a safety hazard. It's a world where shipping
open-weights models fast and to everyone is the only safe strategy - which, conveniently,
means that the safest possible world is one where Meta can execute its roadmap
unimpeded.

posts.text: Why are Snap, LinkedIn, and Substack turning away from slop while Meta and TikTok embrace it? It comes down to what the platforms promise their user bases https://www.platformer.news/slop-restrictions-linkedin-substack-snap/

media.alt:
This summer, we appear to be moving into slop's third era. The first was characterized by
near-universal disdain for laughable writing and six-fingered humans; the second by the
surprising popularity of slop shows like "Fruit Love Island." In the third era of slop, platforms
are rethinking their approaches to Al-generated content based on what their user bases
need from them — and vice-versa. Platforms that place a premium on trust are realizing
just how quickly slop can erode it. And platforms that don't are ready to give us as much
slop as we can handle.

posts.author: Casey Newton
posts.text: I talked to the CEO of one of the only good AI *product* companies — Chris Pedregal of Granola — about what an AI notetaker learns about a company, and what bosses keep asking him to do with it https://www.platformer.news/granola-chris-pedregal-interview/

media.alt:
Pedregal: I think it's an opportunity if it's bottoms-up, and I think it stresses me out if it's
top-down. If you're saying, I don't think my manager is very good — help me navigate how I
should work with my manager — I think that's great. I think it's empowering. CEOs will ask
us all the time, saying: I want everyone at my company using Granola, and I want access to
all the transcripts and all the notes to run the queries that you're talking about. And we say
no. That's not what the tool is built for. You can set that up if you want, but then you have
to create a company culture and set an expectation, and everyone needs to share their
notes and understand what they're getting into. But there's no backdoor way. I think that's
a slippery slope. If you have a backdoor way for someone in power to use all this context to
make judgment calls in that way, that doesn't feel right to me, and that's not a future we
want to build towards.

posts.text: Wrote about AI denialism on Bluesky https://www.platformer.news/a-big-week-for-ai-denialism/

media.alt:
What all of these arguments have in common is that they serve as invitations to stop
thinking about Al.
Who cares? It's just marketing.
Who cares? They're just doing what they were programmed to.
Who cares? It's not like they're sentient.
I understand the appeal of arguments like these. The implications of an exponential takeoff
in Al capabilities are extremely worrisome. They range from advanced cyberattacks like the
one Hugging Face just endured to job loss, novel bioweapons, expanded systems for
surveillance and repression, and autonomous weaponry. Who wants to think about any of
that, if they don't have to?

posts.author: Casey Newton
posts.text: In the wake of OpenAI's autonomous attack against Hugging Face, I wrote about the promise and limitations of Congress' proposed AI kill switch https://www.platformer.news/openai-agent-sandbox-escape-killswitch-bill/

media.alt:
It's an appealing idea. In a future scenario where one company's models are conducting
multiple ongoing cyberattacks, it would be nice if the government could order that
company to hit the off switch. The bill also represents a step toward creating a working
regulatory regime for powerful models — something the world sorely needs.
At the same time, it's worth pointing out that a kill switch has limits, too. At its root, a
trained model is just data — a collection of numbers that can be copied, torrented, and run
anywhere. If an agent manages to obtain and exfiltrate a copy of its weights, there may be
no central process to terminate. As long as the rogue Al is being hosted on a server
controlled by a lab, a kill switch is a great idea. But it won't always be.
